reasoning_traces.think: The chapter window exposes a fundamental tension between numerical resolution and algebraic stability in axisymmetric Navier-Stokes solvers. At low resolutions (Nr=32), the discretization error is masked by physical viscosity. However, as we refine the grid to Nr=64 and 128, the one-sided collocation at the pole introduces a spurious positive eigenvalue scaling as O(Nr^4). This eigenvalue dictates the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) limit, forcing the explicit RK4 integrator to take exponentially smaller substeps. By Nr=256, the required substep count (820 per physical step) and the sheer magnitude of the positive eigenvalue (4.42e6) render the simulation computationally bankrupt. More critically, this eigenvalue corresponds to a non-dissipative mode—an artifact that injects energy rather than dissipating it. The text explicitly rejects spectral filtering as a remedy because it constitutes an artificial external force, violating the strict conservation laws required by the BKM audit. Instead, the only mathematically sound path forward is a change of variables to the circulation \Gamma = r \cdot u_\theta. This transformation analytically cancels the 1/r^2 geometric singularity at the pole, replacing the unstable collocation with a well-posed boundary condition that satisfies a maximum principle. The verification suite confirms this epistemic shift: tests no longer assert naive physical expectations (like higher viscosity always reducing peak vorticity) but instead rigorously document the divergence of the unregularized scheme and mandate the pole-regular fix.

The shift to circulation variables mirrors historical moves in magnetohydrodynamics to use vector potentials to enforce divergence-free constraints naturally.
